content: 1. Standard precautions are required to prevent exposing hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients to Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). 2. Adults and children who are in contact with HSCT recipients and have known or suspected invasive Hib disease, such as meningitis, bacteremia, or epiglottitis, should be placed under droplet precautions until 24 hours after initiating appropriate antibiotic therapy. After this period, they can transition to standard precautions. 3. Household contacts exposed to individuals with Hib disease who also have contact with HSCT recipients should receive rifampin prophylaxis as per published guidelines. Prophylaxis is necessary if all household contacts under 4 years of age are not fully vaccinated. 4. This recommendation is critical because unvaccinated household contacts under 4 years of age are at increased risk for invasive Hib disease. Rifampin is effective in eliminating Hib carriage and preventing invasive disease. 5. 6. Although there is no direct data on vaccine efficacy in HSCT recipients, Hib conjugate vaccine should be administered to HSCT recipients at 12, 14, and 24 months post-transplant. 7. This vaccine is recommended because most HSCT recipients have low levels of Hib capsular polysaccharide antibodies even 4 months post-transplant, and allogeneic recipients with chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) are at increased risk for infections caused by encapsulated organisms like Hib. 8. HSCT recipients exposed to individuals with Hib disease should be offered rifampin prophylaxis according to published recommendations. 9. Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended to prevent infections caused by encapsulated organisms (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Neisseria meningitidis) in allogeneic recipients with chronic GVHD for as long as active treatment for chronic GVHD is ongoing. 10. Antibiotic selection should be guided by local patterns of antibiotic resistance. 11. Recommendations for preventing Hib infections are the same for allogeneic and autologous HSCT recipients. 12. Recommendations for preventing Hib disease are the same for pediatric and adult HSCT recipients, except that children infected with Hib pneumonia require standard precautions with droplet precautions added for the first 24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotic therapy. 13. Appropriate pediatric doses should be administered for both the Hib conjugate vaccine and rifampin prophylaxis. 14. HSCT candidates should be tested for serum anti-cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG antibodies before transplantation to assess their risk for primary CMV infection and reactivation post-transplant. 15. Only FDA-licensed or approved tests should be used for CMV testing. 16. 17. 18. Even long-term monogamous couples can be discordant for CMV infections. During periods of immunocompromise, sexually active HSCT recipients in monogamous relationships should ask their partners to be tested for serum CMV IgG antibodies. 19. 20. CMV-seronegative recipients of allogeneic stem cell transplants from CMV-seronegative donors should receive only leukocyte-reduced or CMV-seronegative red blood cells or platelets to prevent transfusion-associated CMV infection. 21. Insufficient data exists to recommend leukocyte-reduced or CMV-seronegative blood products for CMV-seronegative recipients with CMV-seropositive donors. 22. Healthcare workers should wear gloves when handling blood products or other potentially contaminated biological materials to prevent CMV transmission to HSCT recipients. 23. HSCT patients known to excrete CMV should be placed under standard precautions for the duration of CMV excretion to avoid possible transmission to CMV-seronegative HSCT recipients and candidates. 24. Physicians should note that CMV excretion can be episodic or prolonged. 25. HSCT recipients at risk for CMV disease post-transplant (e.g., all CMV-seropositive recipients and CMV-seronegative recipients with CMV-seropositive donors) should be placed on a CMV disease prevention program from engraftment until 100 days post-transplant. 26. Physicians should use either prophylaxis or preemptive treatment with ganciclovir for allogeneic recipients. 27. When selecting a CMV disease prevention strategy, physicians should assess the risks and benefits of each strategy, the patient’s needs and condition, and the hospital’s virology laboratory support capabilities. 28. A prophylaxis strategy against early CMV (<100 days post-HSCT) for allogeneic recipients involves administering ganciclovir prophylaxis to all at-risk recipients throughout this period. 29. The induction course of ganciclovir is usually started at engraftment, although a brief prophylactic course can be added during HSCT preconditioning. 30. A preemptive strategy against early CMV (<100 days post-HSCT) is preferred over prophylaxis for CMV-seronegative HSCT recipients of seropositive donor cells due to the low attack rate of active CMV infection when screened or filtered blood product support is used. 31. The preemptive strategy restricts ganciclovir use to patients with evidence of CMV infection post-HSCT. 32. This strategy requires sensitive and specific laboratory tests to rapidly diagnose CMV infection post-HSCT and enable immediate administration of ganciclovir upon detection of CMV infection. 33. Allogeneic recipients at risk should be screened at least once per week from 10 days to 100 days post-HSCT for CMV viremia or antigenemia. 34. HSCT physicians should select one of two diagnostic tests to determine the need for preemptive treatment. 35. Detection of CMV pp65 antigen in leukocytes (antigenemia) is preferred for preemptive treatment screening because it is more rapid and sensitive than culture and has good positive predictive value. 36. Direct detection of CMV-DNA by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is very sensitive but has a low positive predictive value. 37. Plasma CMV-DNA PCR is useful during neutropenia when the number of leukocytes per slide is too low for CMV pp65 antigenemia testing.
